newsitem.title: USA: Union says Goodyear talks failed on four key issues.
newsitem.headline: Union says Goodyear talks failed on four key issues.

text.p: Contract talks between Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. and the union representing 13,000 Goodyear workers who went out on strike Sunday foundered on four key issues, the union said.

The largest U.S. tiremaker and the United Steelworkers of America could not agree on job security, outsourcing, contract revisions and certain partnership arrangements, said union spokesman Curt Brown.
"Those are the issues I can talk about. There are other points. There's a lot of unresolved issues," he said.

The rubber workers at Akron, Ohio-based Goodyear declared a strike Sunday after negotiators were unable to reach agreement on a new three-year contract. The negotiators had been in discussions for two months on neutral turf in a Cincinnati hotel.
"There aren't any talks going on at this time," Brown said.
Goodyear spokesman John Perduyn said talks broke off one minute after midnight and no further negotiations were scheduled.
The strike was the first to hit Goodyear since a 140-day-long work stoppage that paralysed the tire industry in 1976.

On April 1, Goodyear was chosen by the union as its target to set the pattern for 1997 bargaining with the industry in advance of the expiration of Goodyear's three-year labour contract reached in 1994.

Although pattern bargaining was in effect, union workers at Goodyear's largest competitor, Bridgestone Corp., have a contract that extends for another three years. That contract emerged from a lengthy and bitter 1994 strike during which the company used replacement workers and imported tires. The long strike drained the United Rubber Workers' strike fund, leading that union to join the steelworkers.
Contract discussions at Uniroyal-Goodrich, the third of the tire industry's so-called Big Three, recently recessed to await the outcome of the Goodyear talks, Brown said.

The striking workers are employed at nine Goodyear plants in Akron, Ohio, Gadsden, Ala., St. Marys, Ohio, Lincoln, Neb., Topeka, Kansas, Danville, Va., Marysville, Ohio, Union City, Tenn., and Sun Prairie, Wis., Brown said.
"Among other issues, we're very concerned about employee security. We see an erosion of jobs," Brown said.
He said the union also wants "a true partnership (with the company), not just one in name only."
Outsourcing, outside contracting and certain unspecified contract take-aways were also issues, Brown said. "We don't intend to work under a regressive agreement," he said.
Goodyear employs a total of 91,000 people at dozens of plants around the world, including 45 in the United States.

"Goodyear has negotiated in good faith, but has been unable to reach a reasonable solution with the steelworkers. The company's final offer would improve what already is recognised as one of the best compensation packages in the industry," Perduyn said.

He said the union's position would restrict Goodyear's flexibility in running its operations. "The company has no intention of mortgaging its future by agreeing to a contract that would widen a contractual disadvantage with its competitors," Perduyn said.
"Goodyear intends to maintain production during the strike to serve its customers," Perduyn said.
